notes: Forward reaction SMARTS only. Reactant template 0 is always the carried molecule; the
remaining templates are filled from the request's `reagents`, in order, or from the slot's
`default` when the caller leaves it out (water and the like are not worth making the model
name). Every SMARTS here was applied to a real substrate with RDKit and its product asserted
in test/test_route_program.py; nothing is carried on inspection alone. A displacement is written for
Cl, Br and I only: C-F does not go, so an alkyl fluoride resolves its site and then fails to
react, which is the honest answer rather than a product nobody could make.
An entry with `siteSlots` joins two places on ONE carried molecule, so its carried-side pattern
is written as a component group - ([a].[b]) - which RDKit matches only within a single molecule.
`siteSlots` names what each of the two sites must be; `site` is null for such an entry. The
oxidant of a closure is named in `reagents` and the byproduct in the SMARTS matches it, so the
equation balances as written rather than leaving half of it to the reader.

transforms.summary: Hydrolyse an ester to the carboxylic acid, releasing the alcohol.

Esterify a carboxylic acid with an alcohol. The water is the formal condensation byproduct and balances the equation; with a carbodiimide its elements are taken up as the urea instead, so do not also list that urea. On a substrate that also carries a basic amine, acid conditions deliver the ammonium salt rather than the free base, and a following acylation needs a stoichiometric base.

Couple a carboxylic acid with an amine to the amide (a coupling agent or the acyl chloride). The water is the formal condensation byproduct and balances the equation; with a carbodiimide its elements are taken up as the urea instead, so do not also list that urea.
Hydrolyse an amide to the carboxylic acid, releasing the amine.
Acylate a free amine with an acyl chloride, releasing HCl. The HCl is taken up by a stoichiometric base the toolkit supplies, without which it salts the amine and stops the reaction.
Reduce a ketone to the secondary alcohol (NaBH4, LiAlH4 or H2). Written as the formal hydrogen addition so the equation balances; the summary names the reagent actually used.
Reduce an aldehyde to the primary alcohol (NaBH4 or H2). Written as the formal hydrogen addition so the equation balances.
Oxidise a secondary alcohol to the ketone (PCC, Swern or Dess-Martin).
Oxidise a primary alcohol to the aldehyde (PCC, Swern or Dess-Martin).
Oxidise an aldehyde to the carboxylic acid (KMnO4 or Ag2O).
Reduce a nitro group to the primary amine (H2/Pd or Fe/HCl), releasing two equivalents of water. Three equivalents of hydrogen are written as reactants so the equation balances.
Hydrolyse a nitrile to the carboxylic acid, releasing ammonia.
Hydrogenate an alkene to the alkane (H2/Pd-C). The hydrogen is written as a reactant so the equation balances.
Displace an alkyl halide with an amine, releasing the hydrogen halide.
O-alkylate a phenol with an alkyl halide, releasing the hydrogen halide.
Convert a carboxylic acid to the acyl chloride (SOCl2 or oxalyl chloride).
Oxidise two thiols on one molecule to the disulfide with iodine, closing a ring and releasing two equivalents of hydrogen iodide.
Alkylate two thiols on one molecule with a bis(halomethyl)arene, closing a ring the arene bridges and releasing two equivalents of the hydrogen halide.

Remove the carbamate protecting group from the amine, whichever one is there: the toolkit picks fmoc-removal, boc-removal or cbz-removal by what the carried molecule actually carries, so a route never has to track which group it installed. It refuses when the molecule carries two different ones, and then you name the specific removal.
Remove an Fmoc carbamate from the amine (piperidine), releasing dibenzofulvene and carbon dioxide.

Remove a Boc carbamate from the amine (TFA or HCl), releasing isobutylene and carbon dioxide. The acid delivers the amine as its ammonium salt, which is not nucleophilic until a base liberates it; the following acylation is supplied with a stoichiometric base.
Remove a Cbz carbamate from the amine by hydrogenolysis (H2/Pd-C), releasing toluene and carbon dioxide. The hydrogen is written as a reactant so the equation balances.
Cleave a benzyl ester to the carboxylic acid by hydrogenolysis (H2/Pd-C), releasing toluene. The hydrogen is written as a reactant so the equation balances.

Cleave a tert-butyl ester to the carboxylic acid (TFA), releasing isobutylene. On a substrate that also carries a free amine the acid delivers it as the ammonium salt, which a following acylation must liberate with a base.

Cleave a 3-methylpent-3-yl (OMpe) ester to the carboxylic acid (TFA), releasing 2-ethyl-1-butene. The hindered tertiary ester is the usual aspartimide precaution on an aspartate side chain; it is cleaved under the same acid as a tert-butyl ester, more slowly. On a substrate that also carries a free amine the acid delivers it as the ammonium salt, which a following acylation must liberate with a base.

Protect a free amine as its carbamate with a chloroformate (Cbz-Cl, Fmoc-Cl), releasing HCl. The HCl is taken up by a stoichiometric base the toolkit supplies, without which it salts the amine and stops the reaction.

Acylate the carried molecule's free amine with a carboxylic acid (a coupling agent such as DCC/HOBt with a stoichiometric tertiary base). The C-to-N direction: the growing chain is carried and the incoming acid is the reagent. The water is the formal condensation byproduct and balances the equation; with a carbodiimide its elements are taken up as the urea instead, so do not also list that urea.
Remove a trityl group from a side-chain thiol (TFA with a scavenger), releasing triphenylmethanol.

Protect a thiol as its S-trityl thioether with trityl chloride, releasing HCl. The HCl is taken up by a stoichiometric base the toolkit supplies. Removed by s-trityl-removal, which runs on acid and water and gives triphenylmethanol - the two are not the same equation.
Remove a trityl group from a side-chain nitrogen (TFA with a scavenger), releasing triphenylmethanol.

Protect a primary carboxamide - an asparagine or glutamine side chain - as its N-trityl amide with trityl chloride, releasing HCl. This is the side-chain mask that keeps a coupling activator from dehydrating the amide to the nitrile. Removed by n-trityl-removal.

Remove a trityl group from an imidazole ring nitrogen (TFA with a scavenger), releasing triphenylmethanol. The freed ring nitrogen keeps its hydrogen, which a rule written for an aliphatic nitrogen cannot express.
Remove a trityl group, wherever it sits: the toolkit picks the thiol, nitrogen or imidazole rule by what the carried molecule actually carries.
Cleave a tert-butyl ether to the alcohol or phenol (TFA), releasing isobutylene. A tert-butyl ester is left alone; it has its own transformation.

Protect an alcohol or phenol as its tert-butyl ether by acid-catalysed addition of isobutylene. Nothing is released: the alkene simply adds across the O-H bond, which makes this the exact reverse of tert-butyl-ether-removal.
Remove the Pbf sulfonyl from an arginine guanidine (TFA), releasing the sulfonic acid.

Remove a 2,4-dimethoxybenzyl (Dmb) group from a backbone amide nitrogen with acid and water, releasing 2,4-dimethoxybenzyl alcohol and restoring the N-H. Dmb is carried on the glycine of an Fmoc-Asp(OtBu)-(Dmb)Gly-OH dipeptide, where its job is to remove the very N-H that closes onto the aspartate ester to give the aspartimide; it comes off in the same TFA cleavage as the side-chain groups.

Open a pseudoproline back to the native serine, threonine or cysteine residue with acid and water, releasing the ketone. The oxazolidine is a cyclic N,O-acetal, so hydrolysis restores BOTH the side-chain hydroxyl and the backbone N-H - the point of a pseudoproline is that the kink it puts in the chain is temporary, and the residue the route was asked for is the one that comes back.

Release the chain from the solid support, cleaving the ester that held it and giving the free C-terminal acid. The chain is the piece carrying map 2, the ester oxygen that stays with the acid; map 1 is the support itself, which the route does not follow.
Join the free N-terminal amine to the free C-terminal acid of one chain, closing the backbone to a macrolactam and releasing water.
